title: How "Free Money" Breeds Shadow IT
author: Artur Henriques
summary: Artur Henriques, writing for IT managers in medium and large companies, argues that the real budget game is played through internal recharges, the way departments charge one another for services. His central claim is that "free money", a multi-year transformation budget that quietly funds ongoing operations, lets other departments hire IT skills and build software outside IT governance, which is how Shadow IT is born. Because no recharge occurs, the software feels free to its users while the company pays for poor oversight and eventually needs IT to maintain it. He recommends three responses: avoid vanity projects when requesting budget, transfer operating funds to IT whenever it is asked to onboard a Shadow IT tool, and lead by example by mastering finance so that IT can demand the same rigor from others. The essay treats this as internal politics that is messy and a root cause of conflict, and its practical lesson is that perpetual project budgets are a lack of management rather than project management.
points: The visible annual budgeting game sits on top of a second game of internal recharges, which is where the real flow of money and influence is decided.
"Free money" project budgets that renew indefinitely mask operating costs as projects and let departments avoid paying IT for software they need.
Shadow IT emerges when departments hire technical skills to build tools outside IT governance, and the company pays later through poor oversight and unsupported systems.
When IT is asked to onboard such software, the funding should transfer to the IT budget so the maintenance cost lands on whoever commissioned the tool.
Leaders gain standing to demand rigor from others only after running their own budgets with finance-grade discipline.
quotes: In Medium and Large Companies a political game determines how the organization operates and how things actually get done.
These internal recharges are how the real game is played. It is where decision-makers and department heads find creative ways to let initiatives fly under the radar when they lack a dedicated budget.
The problem begins when that “project” becomes a multi-year endeavor with ongoing efforts. Operational costs are masked as “projects”, and no internal recharge really happens.
This is one of the ways Shadow IT is born: when other departments manage to hire IT skills to produce software that is not under IT governance.

A lack of internal recharges shows a lack of structure and control over how money is spent inside the company. Assigning budget lines with multi-year renewals on a perpetual basis is not project management. It is a lack of management altogether.
If someone is doing software for “free”, they will eventually need the capabilities of an IT department for maintenance and support.
If your castle is well maintained, it is natural to demand the same level of rigor from other departments.
